title: "${var}"/"${expr}" string interpolation is deprecated
summary: PHP 8.2 deprecates the "${var}" and "${expr}" curly-brace string interpolation syntaxes in favor of "$var"/"{$var}" and "{${expr}}".
new_code_policy: Never write "${var}" or "${expr}" interpolation in double-quoted strings or heredocs; use "$var"/"{$var}" for a plain variable and "{${expr}}" for the general expression form (most commonly variable variables).
existing_code_policy: Rewrite "${var}"/"${expr}" occurrences opportunistically to their replacement forms. Each occurrence still parses and runs on every currently known minor (8.2-8.5), but emits a deprecation notice on 8.2 and later, so leaving it in place is a growing source of deprecation noise rather than an immediate break.
guideline: Prefer "$var" (or "{$var}" when the following characters would otherwise be parsed as part of the variable name) for a simple variable, and "{${expr}}" when the interpolated part is an arbitrary expression such as a variable variable ("${$name}"). Do not use the bare "${...}" curly-brace form inside double-quoted strings or heredocs.
details: PHP 8.2 deprecated the curly-brace string interpolation forms "${name}" (a plain variable) and "${expr}" (an arbitrary expression, most often a variable variable such as "${$name}") when used inside double-quoted strings and heredocs, per the accepted RFC deprecate_dollar_brace_string_interpolation. The unaffected, recommended replacements are "$name"/"{$name}" for the simple case and "{${expr}}" for the expression case. This is a syntax-level deprecation only: it changes which interpolation spelling the parser accepts without a deprecation notice, not what a correctly rewritten program does at runtime.
notes: The 8.2 UPGRADING notes state that removal is planned for PHP 9, but an announced future removal is not yet an established fact (ADR-005), so removed_in stays null here until a released PHP 9 UPGRADING file actually states it; this note exists to record the plan without treating it as a lifecycle fact.

The "${expr}" form is most commonly seen as variable-variable interpolation, e.g. "${$name}"; its direct replacement is "{${$name}}", not "{$name}", because the inner "$name" must still be evaluated as an expression rather than read literally.
